issues.legal_issue: A state authority that fails to decide a mining-lease application within the prescribed period cannot later grant that application when the applicable rules treat the failure as a refusal.
material_facts: An applicant sought a mining lease, and the application remained undisposed of beyond the period applicable to pending applications.
The state authority later granted the lease after that period had expired.
The central revisional authority set the grant aside on the basis that the application had been deemed refused.
issues.conclusion: The failure to decide within the prescribed period amounted to refusal for the purposes of the rules, and the state authority was incompetent to grant the lease after the period expired.
issues.legal_principle: Reading rules 28(1-A) and 57(2) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 together, the deemed refusal operates for the purposes of the rules generally, not merely to permit an application for review. The state authority therefore loses power to deal with the application after the prescribed period. Dey Gupta & Company v. State of Bihar was referred to, but its contrary view that the authority retained power to decide after the period was not accepted.

rule.if: mining_lease_application and decision_deadline_expired and application_undisposed and applicable_rules_treat_failure_as_refusal

predicates.mining_lease_application: An applicant sought a mining lease from a state authority.
predicates.decision_deadline_expired: The time allowed for the state authority to decide the application passed.
predicates.application_undisposed: The state authority had not decided the application by the end of the allowed period.
predicates.applicable_rules_treat_failure_as_refusa: The applicable rules treated failure to decide within the allowed period as a refusal for the purposes of those rules.

issues.definition: When a mining-lease application remained undecided after the deadline and the applicable rules treated that failure as a refusal, the state authority lacked power to grant it afterward.

issues.legal_issue: A government representation that an application remains pending cannot prevent application of a mandatory statutory rule that deems the application refused after the decision period expires.
material_facts: In court proceedings, a government advocate represented that the applicant's lease application was still pending and that the state government would decide it on the merits.
The application had remained undecided beyond the period prescribed by the applicable rules.
The state government later granted the lease, and the High Court relied on the representation in concluding that the state could not contend that the application had been refused.
issues.conclusion: The representation could not change the legal effect of the rules or confer power on the state government to act contrary to them; there can be no estoppel against a statute.
issues.legal_principle: Rules 28(1-A) and 57(2) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1949 are statutory rules that bind the government and cannot be waived by it. A representation by a government advocate cannot alter their requirements or confer authority inconsistent with them.

predicates.mining_lease_application: An applicant sought a mining lease from a state authority.
predicates.mandatory_rule_governs_application: A mandatory rule governed how or when the state authority could decide the application.
predicates.government_represented_application_as_pe: A government representative told a court that the application remained pending.

issues.definition: When a mandatory rule governed a mining-lease application, a government representation that it remained pending did not prevent the government from applying that rule.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory revisional authority may review a state grant made in compliance with a mandamus when that authority was not a party to the mandamus proceeding and applies its own statutory duties.
material_facts: A court issued a mandamus directing the state government to dispose of a lease application; the central government and another applicant were not parties to that proceeding.
The state government considered the application and granted the lease in compliance with the mandamus.
The central government, acting as the statutory revisional authority on another applicant's review application, set the grant aside under the applicable rules.
issues.conclusion: The mandamus bound the state government, but it did not bind the central government or the other applicant; the central government could discharge its statutory revisional duties without infringing the mandamus.
issues.legal_principle: The mandamus was not a judgment in rem and did not bind persons or authorities that were not parties to the proceeding. The central government, as a quasi-judicial revisional authority created by the statutory rules, remained bound to discharge its duties under rule 57. Its review of the state grant did not violate the mandamus, which the state had already obeyed by considering the application. Justice Shah dissented on this issue, reasoning that the central government could not in effect sit in appeal over the High Court's order.

rule.if: statutory_review_of_lease_grant and state_grant_followed_mandamus and reviewing_authority_not_party_to_mandamus and mandamus_directed_state_to_consider_application

predicates.statutory_review_of_lease_grant: A statutory revisional authority was asked to review a state authority's lease grant.
predicates.state_grant_followed_mandamus: The state authority made the grant after acting in compliance with a court order.
predicates.reviewing_authority_not_party_to_mandamu: The authority later asked to review the grant was not a party to the proceeding in which the court order issued.
predicates.mandamus_directed_state_to_consider_appl: The court order directed the state authority to consider or dispose of an application.

issues.definition: When a state grant followed a mandamus directing the state to consider an application and the statutory reviewing authority was not a party to that proceeding, the reviewing authority could review the grant under its governing rules.
